title: Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon®
text: The bottom line is that the original Ghost Recon remains as the best release in the entire series. The game shines in the non-linear, non-restrictive gameplay that has plagued many linear corridor shooters (to include Ghost Recon Future Soldier). Players have a map, and a team of men, and must apply critical thinking through mission analysis in order to be successful. The game also has an outstanding damage model that still outshines most shooters; A single 5.56mm round will kill, and players can sustain arm and leg wounds that affect their ability to shoot and move. Third person animations also reflect player damage in the form of limping and visible blood stains and gunshot wounds. There is also an RPG-like system that allows players to develop their Ghosts and apply personal attributes that will improve their performance. My only big gripe is the use of a reticule system instead of a first person weapon. Unlike Ravenshield, there is no on-screen, first person weapon. There are only a series of recitules that can be zoomed in to simulate weapon sights.

text: I've come around to this game after a few false starts. I definitely recommend getting the 2.0 mod for this game, as it's a vast improvement over the original layout. On to the game: I'm sure you've heard this game takes place in two parts - planning and action. Both are incredibly well done and are borderline simulation territory, but definitely still very gamey. The AI is pretty good, but not perfect. You can tell your squad to go clear a room and sometimes they will bunch in the doorway, ignoring terrorists. Another favorite is missions where enemies may not be armed, but are trying to complete some objective (like deleting data from computers). Many times, the AI would be told to clear a room and ignore these enemies, leading to a mission failure. For this reason, I feel there are a few missions that are just bugged and don't reflect the base game (namely mission 11, where it's unclear what is causing a mission failure, as all weapons were silenced and all enemies were killed upon entering a room). For missions like these, it's nice to have access to the developer console and just 'completemission.' This game is far from perfect, but it's really fun when everything comes together. The Gold Edition comes with the expansions, too, so you get a lot (around 30 missions?) for your money. SWAT 3 and 4 are still my favs, but this has an addicting element to it, as well.

title: Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six® 3 Gold
text: If you ever felt like FPS games today were just shooting galleries, then you should probably pick up this game. I was there, I fought the war against Supersoldier-Nazi-Terrorists from the future. I played Rainbow Six on the console and I beat it once... only once. The game has you playing against Supersoldier-Nazi-terrorists from the future, seriously you should watch the intro... that's the only way I can explain the story, for America. You thought CoD: World at War was deep? This game is deeper. This game is about fighting for America.... in Switzerland. As a fun, challenging game, Rainbow Six has you taking control of up to three teams and with you planning out their movements along with placing checkpoints yourself. As you start the mission and having your teams following their pre-constructed paths, they will all inevitably die to the incredible aim of the Super-soldier-Nazi-Terrorists (I always manually take control of teams and members to make sure no one dies). Still, it was much easier than the console version which basically had you and three other guys (or four, I forgot) with no backup and running into a whole lotta crossfires and traps. Men get blown to pieces by Terrorists with their grenades and you will get cutdown mercilessly by molten metal fired from the barrels of hidden guns. This game is easier, with the ability to pre-plan your movements and the ability to take control of multiple teams and team members. This game isn't about twitch shooting or aim, it's about precaution. Precaution as in, "Don't run in clear view of a sniper you dumb♥♥♥♥." The game doesn't hold your hand and requires a lot of luck at times, but in all honesty it is how you plan and how you plan to execute it along with a plan B if everything goes wrong. If you find firefights too frustrating, the game even allows aim assist (the equivalent of aimbotting). You have to anticipate the ♥♥♥♥♥iest situations and how to deal with them. I like the weapons, most of them have different stats and have situational advantages during some missions. However, shotguns are completely inaccurate unless you've got a scope on it (which I find strange). Team members also have stats and it somewhat rewards you for keeping them alive. The more men survive through missions the better stats they get, so they can aim better, run better, etc. Always keep stealth team members with other stealth team members otherwise the other dudes in the group will give them away. Having a balanced number of team members and organizing their equipment is actually.... fun. I get to choose what weapon to use, what grenades I want and who I want with me. Yeah, the game can get frustrating at times, but mostly it is your fault if you lose. You have to observe enemy movement, study their patrol paths and watch them intently then plan actions accordingly. You can't run in every room throwing a smoke grenade because of your limited supplies. The heartbeat sensors actually make the game easier because you can see where terrorists are going through the walls and doors (console game had thermal vision). You're never supposed to fight the enemy head-on not unless you've put yourself in a advantageous situation (i.e. smoked room enemy can't see you, flash bang renders terrorists unable to fight back etc.). Multiplayer is also a blast, if you ever get to play just use your Uplay account username and password. I had to play with three or so other guys against hordes of terrorists in the other room with us throwing tear gas this way and that. There are plenty of wonderful pvp and pve levels that has you killing terrorists on top of buildings, in cities, on boats and wherever the strange and unique level designs take you. Did I tell you I got to fight Nazi Terrorists... IN SPACE?! Go buy it but keep in mind it's tough difficulty and sometimes frustrating nature.

title: Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six® 3 Gold
text: Truthful in its nature of strategy and action, R63 is quite undeniably the last true tactical game to have come in the series. Pitting you in a what-would-be a spec op's worst nightmare scenarios too crazy for real-life, you're given simple objectives that usually encompasses rescuing hostages, preventing certain destruction, and all the while killing everyone else in sight (enemies do rarely surrender though). The levels are great and complex, but some may prove to be too much of a challenge, with some of the most unforgivingly tough gun combat you'll face. As hard as it can get, this instead left me craving for more for some reason. Enjoyment is however, marred by a few technicalities to the likes of the occasional dumb but crazy aimbotting enemy AI and slightly underwhelming gunplay. What's more annoying is the incompetency of your own teammates, who may fare well in the easier levels but get completely obliterated in certain, more assault-oriented levels. Ultimately it doesn't matter how much strategic map planning comes into play, it all boils down to the player's own level of FPS skills for the best success, which puts into question the real importance of the aspect. Regardless, this game goes far behind SWAT 4 as one of the best tactical shooter I've ever played. And given the state of the Tactical Shooter genre that has since died off in gaming trend, this position will always remain as such, sadly.

title: Tom Clancy’s The Division™
text: When I first saw previews of The Division I was simply blown away. The wait for the game became simply excruciating. At the time I couldn't imagine a game that I wanted to play more. Then time passed, slowly my excitement waned, and it released. I forgot about it. It wasn't until a good while after it launched that I realized it was already out. So I read reviews to see how great it was (it must be...right?) They didn't have nice things to say. And so, bummed out, I passed on it. Fast forward to a few years later, I took some medicine that I will not disclose the name of but just tell you that it can severely impair your judgement and woke up the next day with no memory of the night before and got on my computer to find The Division (and several other games) in my library. Great... I zombie-bought all these games. I figured I should at least try The Division up to two hours before refunding it so that I can at least see for myself what is wrong with it. The short answer; nothing at all. It's superb. The long answer; from what I've gathered, Massive/Ubisoft have updated and polished the game so well having had enough time that it easily the best game of it's kind. (Looking at you Destiny) There is a plethora of extremely diverse and engaging end-game content thanks partly to all the amazing additions added with the DLC, a particular standout being the Survival game mode. But the base game without the DLC has a great amount/variety of end-game content too. Plus, everything leading up to end game is fantastic as well, some would even argue it's the best part of the game but I disagree as I enjoy the end-game loot quest more. I highly suggest buying the game and the DLC if you are a fan of the genre as it perfects the formula and most critically, in comparison to other genre leader Destiny, it actually has a tangible end-game that isn't some short, shallow pathetic excuse of an end-game for casuals. I rate it a 9/10

text: I was playing this game on the free weekend and was stunned how well it is. I never really considered playing it, because the reviews I read were kinda bad. (Not sure if I only read Steam reviews or also professional ones though.) But after I played a few hours I had to buy it while it still was on sale, got it in Uplay though. And I am still playing it after 14 hours or something, I even bought the Season Pass (you don't really need it as beginner though, it's rather endgame stuff - buy it on sale). Most of the time I am playing alone and enjoy to dwell in this dark atmosphere of the game, but am also looking forward to play with some other Agents soon. I really love this postapocalyptic setting, although the feel of deadlyness of this new world with the most destructive flu virus you can imagine, could been made a bit more scary imho. I mean this is almost a Zombie apocalypse setting, regarding the world it's playing in. I guess Ubisoft rather wanted a Sci-Fi Thriller than a Horror game probably, so they went this (a bit softer) way. But no problem, it's still a very cool presentation. Nevertheless the game is really atmospheric and the grafics are looking awesome, I was surprised how well it is looking at stable 60FPS on my machine. It's a mix between an online MMO and a tactical shooter, with RPG-like exp points and levels, perks, etc. But it's foremost  a postapocalyptic 3rd person shooter. I think it's the first of it's kind in this composition. Looking forward to the year 2 content! P.S. if you read this, Ubisoft, please add more variety to agents in the character creation. title: Tom Clancy’s The Division™
text: It's a real pity Ubisoft can't help but kick themselves in the d**k every time they go and promote a game, because The Division is an excellent looter-shooter set in an impeccably recreated New York City, that was crippled from the get go by Ubisoft's abysmal marketing practices. The world is, in a word, stunning. I've never seen attention to detail on a scale such as this. NYC seems to be recreated at an almost 1:1 scale, and there are hundreds of alleyways, buildings, and streets to explore and investigate. I don't understand the technology that's gone into optimising this experience, but suffice it to say that I get no hitching or frame rate drops at all, and the world (and in particular, the weather and night effects) look amazing. Balanced difficulty scaling, rewarding end-game loot pursuits, and a constant roll-out of new things to do are matched with an excellent implimentation of drop-in multiplayer mechancics to create a game that is almost as fun to play alone as it is with other people. The balance of gameplay and difficulty means that teamwork is highly rewarding without ever leaving you feeling like you're not pulling your weight. The Dark Zone is a truly engaging and tense experiment that becomes more rewarding as you level up, and while griefing is possible, it is rare that you run into people that are individually impossible to defeat. My advice is to travel in teams, but once you pass lvl 30 the difficulty levels out and the are becomes much more open to single-player engagement and exploration. My only wish is that there were more players. Hopefully this may convince you to drop some cash on it, because it is well worth the expense.

title: Tom Clancy’s The Division™
text: This review is based solely on solo play since the main reason I've bought it is for single player experience. PROS: - Good shooting and cover mechanics - Great graphics with quite steady performance (played on i7-6700, GTX1060, 32GB RAM, Win10 64bit) - Decent looting, skill & perk upgrading, gear crafting/customization - You could easily get 20+ hours out of story/side missions, and many more if you're into PVE/PVP. - Multiplayer is convenient. You do match-making before entering a mission area and you don't have to stick with the party once you're done with the mission. It gives you freedom. CONS: - You're always online. The server may randomly kick you out mid-mission without any rhyme or reason. It happened to me a couple of times in one day and my internet connection was solid. When you get back in the game, you start at the last checkpoint. - If you don't like repetitive missions and grinding, this game may not be for you. FACTS: - This is an RPG with shooting elements; not a shooter with RPG elements. It follows MMO RPG formula. A bullet-sponge enemy that once kill you in 2 seconds will become an easy prey when you level up and have better gears. And since this is an RPG, grinding and repetition is part of the formula. So if you don't enjoy grinding or teaming up with other players,  pass this one up. - I know that there's a lot of hate for Uplay, but it doesn't really affect anything. OVERALL: It's worth the sale price for me. I'm enjoying it and I'll try PVE later once I finish the campaign.

title: Tom Clancy’s The Division™
text: This review if for version 1.7.1 Pros: +Looter/Shooter +Co-op +Lots to do +Lots of loot +Demo to try before buy +Level up system with skills/talents/perks tree +PvE and PvP +Build a base as you progress +Gear progression +Cosmetic dress up +Dungeons and bosses Cons: -Awkward gameplay -Matchmaking system -Reach end game before DLC -Uneven Difficulty -Enemies can be bullet sponges Tom Clancy's The Division is a cover based looter/shooter.  If you liked the Borderlands series this could be something you should try out.  The entire game takes place in New York City and someone has released a mutated small pox virus and is killing everyone!  Your job, in The Division, is to find out who released this and put a stop to them. First and foremost this game was fun, LONG, challenging and rewarding.  I enjoyed Borderlands so this one was a no brainer.  The game took me roughly 60 hours to 100% complete.  I completed all the quests and found all the collectables. The difficulty in this game was all over the place.  At one moment you're over powered and the next you die in two bullets.  If you get surrounded chances are you'll die.  There are safe houses all over the world so if you do die and there isn't a respawn point you won't be too far away.  During your adventure there are loot boxes all over the world and all the enemies drop loot too. Loot consists of two primary weapons and a side arm.  There are backpacks to hold more gear and armor pieces like gloves, chest pieces, knee pads and more!  Gear is standard like you've been accustomed to throughout other games.  You have your grey gear (worst), then green gear, blue gear, purple gear, yellow gear and finally a pinkish color gear (best).  Each progression in color provides better stats and additional perks.  Finally, there's cosmetics.  Cosmetics don't provide any benefit and is strictly there for looks.  These drop in loot boxes and from enemies as well. The cover based system was something I'm neutral over.  Sometimes it works fine and other times it didn't and when it didn't I died.  In example:  When I was in cover and I wanted to move in cover I'd sometimes come out of cover.  I also had certain times where my skills wouldn't work.  It must had been positioning while I was in cover.  As you level up in the game you can pick different skills, talents and perks to use and change at any time for FREE!  You can also repair and build up a home base.  You'll get more skills doing this as well. You can pick skills that make you a Tank, DPS or a Healer.  When you reach end game you will get gear that have set bonus'.  When you reach this part this is when the grind comes in to play.  There are daily missions and weekly missions.  Each give you random gear to help complete your gear sets.  You can do a lot of the game solo, but certain missions will need to be done through the matchmaking system.  You can use the matchmaking system to queue up with 3 others (4 in total) to play through the games "dungeons". I hated the matchmaking system.  While leveling I'd queue for a match, but start before anyone joined.  I only got lucky a couple of times for someone to join my game.  All other times no one joined or joined at the very end of my 20-40 mins session.  By the time I reached end game this didn't change and was sitting idle in matchmaking for quite some time before I just cancelled out. In my opinion the matchmaking system needs to be reworked. There is a PvP system and an area strictly for it called The Dark Zone.  You can solo the areas or group up just like in PvE.  There will be random NPC's that you can kill in The Dark Zone, but real people are in there too so watch your six!  If you find gear/weapons while in the Dark Zone you must signal a helicopter to extract your findings.  While the helicopter is extracting you must protect it.  If you die during this process you will lose PvP experiance and the gear you found will drop and can be picked up by anyone. There are a lot of things to do once you reach level 30 (max level), but you must wait until then to do so.  All the DLC is locked behind level 30.  As I previously said it took me 60 hours to get there, but that's because of completionist.  I wished they'd space end game DLC out better instead of only at the end. I had a lot of fun regardless of the problems I had and the enemies could at times take way to long to kill, but a good game nonetheless.  The game regularly goes on sale for $20, but you can also grab the gold edition which includes the base game with all the DLC for $38.  That price is well worth it as you'll get plenty of game time and even more so with friends playing coop.  Worth a single playthrough and definitely a try.  8/10

title: Tomb Raider II
text: Lara “Don't you think you've seen enough” Croft Another great entry in the series and for many the benchmark for all other TR games, Tomb Raider II is a bigger and tougher sequel with more adventures and puzzles that are going to push the player’s skills and logic to the limit. Set after the hijinks of the first game, Lara is now on a hunt for the secret treasure that might grant the power of the Dragon to its user. She wants to hide it from getting into the wrong hands; while a mysterious cult at the same time is trying to retrieve what they think belongs to them and rule the world of course.  Set across 18 levels and many locations around the globe, you will visit the treacherous Great Wall, the breathtaking streets of Venice, secret installations, ancient Tibet monasteries and a sunken ship at the bottom of the ocean. Lara has a couple of new moves, such as rollback in mid air while jumping, rollback while underwater, and a gracious swan dive, along with new weapons to make the combat a bit more interesting, such as automatic pistols, grenade launcher and M16. Levels this time are bigger, more complex and more demanding, as you’ll have to use every single move set and the right weapon on the right enemy to reach the end. Graphics wise, everything has more polygons than TR1, including Lara, but new players will hardly notice a difference from the previous game.  Music and sound effects are perfect, as they show up at the right time to bolster the player when meeting a tough challenge ahead or to warn them to be careful due to many dangers nearby. There are still some archaic drawbacks to the game: combat is still very primitive with its bullet-spungy enemies even though the new weapons make it less tedious; some levels and situations are a bit illogical and demand a suspension of belief, such as underwater levels that have mooks in them. Yes, there are a couple of levels inside the Titanic-like ship that is hundreds of meters below water, and enemies are there just waiting for you there with no stockpiles or a transport back to the surface. I can already image this situation: Generic Enemy 1: Are you sure Lara is going to show here? I mean it’s cold and rusty here and the damn ship could fall apart every second? Generic Enemy 2: Don’t sweat it! She’ll be here soon with a prescribed led poisoning! Generic Enemy 1: But what after we stop here? We didn’t brought food or anything to pull us out of here? Generic Enemy 2: Hey, looks at bright side! If we die here, I’m sure our boss is going to pay to our families a handsome MIA insurance that was guaranteed in the contract. Generic Enemy 1: You mean the contract we never signed? Generic Enemy 2: Yep! Our boss has thought of everything. Generic Enemy 1: But I don’t have any family! That’s why I’m here with you guys at the bottom of the ocean floor with no equipment or supplies whatsoever. Generic Enemy 2: Then you don’t have nothing to worry about, friend! Your destiny is in good hands. Even with its shortcomings, the new adventures of Lara Croft more than successfully deliver that Indiana Jones vibe. Tomb Raider II gets two thumbs recommendation from me and it’s a classic piece of gaming history everyone should try. It is easily among the best ones in this franchise.

text: I'm just gonna come right out and say it. The controls ruin the game for me. Twenty hours between the first game and this one; the controls still don't feel natural. In fact, pretty much every problem I have with the game (much like the first game) can be traced back to the controls. It's not even the same case as something like Dark Souls, La-Mulana, or even Gunvalkyrie where the control scheme is just different and you get used to it after an hour or two. I do get it, though. I do get why this game is still so well-received. It's because of the people who played it back in the day. I'll admit it; I'm the same way with Glover. Lotsa people hate that game for the controls, but I think they're just fine. I also admit that the reason why I can get the controls to work is because I played it so much when I was younger. As for Tomb Raider, this is my first time with the series. I didn't grow up with it, so I came into the series as an outsider. Again, as far as everything else goes, I quite liked it. The puzzles are great, the atmosphere was incredible in the first game, especially when things go all Lovecraftian. The platforming and combat... could've been great as well, had the controls been better. However, when even after 20 some hours I still haven't gotten used to the controls, I don't think that's a problem on my end. That's why I can't recommend this game to first-timers of the series. It seems like a petty complaint, but once again, all of the problems I've had with the past two games stem from the controls. I won't give this a score, as I haven't completed the game. I don't think I will in the future, either. Here's to hoping I can enjoy Tomb Raider 3.

Meaning no young witch in colourful fairy forests but a hellish wayfarer traversing Giger's versino of Burning Man. Check out the screenshots. If you'd like to spend a few hours puzzling about in these worlds, Tormentum will not disappoint. As far as light adventures go, you got solid puzzles and above average sound effects. But again, those graphics... There aren't lots of games with an artistic vision coming so vividly to ludic (un)life. Rating: Beksinski's spectre raises 4 out of 5 tumbs from demi-hell.

text: I'll start off by saying I really don't want to give this a thumbs down, but unfortunately Steam doesn't have a "On the fence" button. So instead I'll just cut to the chase. VISUALS: -If you enjoy dark fantasy and surreal art- the gothic, the baroque, the grotesque- GET THIS GAME. - If you like art in games, hope to make art for games, or just like creativity in games and want inspiration- GET THIS. - If you're a fan of Giger or Beksinski, DEFINITELY GET THIS GAME. I don't really have to go into detail on this. The screenshots speak for themselves. LENGTH: The game is very short. This is a 3 to 4 hour game, sans any mucking about in confusion. Not really a detriment in its own right, but definitely a factor to consider. GAMEPLAY/PUZZLES: The game isn't challenging. I can't remember the last time I played a point and click game, but I still breezed through this. This could be seen as a blessing for casual players just looking to experience the art firsthand, but I'm certain it would be underwhelming for any seasoned point-and-click fan. WRITING: It's lackluster. It's not awful, but considering what the game was trying to do it needed to do much better here. I'll avoid spoilers but it’s important to know that the writing in the game is inseparable from moral choice. The story, the theme and the visuals of the game ultimately revolve around death, sins, punishment and things not being what they seem. This could have been incredible, but for a game so trenched in morality, it is portrayed as very black and white. There are two endings to this game and around 7 moral choices you must make. They're fairly rudimentary , and even doing two perceived 'bad' choices will give you the bad ending. Morality is very complicated and needs to be handled as such if your whole story hinges on exploring these themes. Games like Silent Hill 2, Spec Ops: The Line and The Walking Dead all accomplished this with flying colors, and had that quality of writing gone into a game like this the end result would have been haunting. Of this I have no doubt. As it stands however, the end result is this world of beautiful visuals and unsettling atmosphere that winds up being in the service of a lot of nothing. If you're looking for a great story, interesting characters or strong worldbuilding (particularly revolving around morality and the darkness in the human heart), you will be disappointed. OVERALL: I bought the game on impulse and my choice to buy it was exclusively rooted in the artwork. I didn't go in with any other expectations so personally, I'm happy with what I got out of it and do no regret anything. But I cannot say with confidence that this would be the case with somebody else so I leave it at this: If you came here for the art- go for it. An art book or ticket to a gallery show or museum often cost way more than 12$, and here the art is interactive. That's just awesome. You can't do much better than that. Just don't expect much else from it.

title: Tormentum - Dark Sorrow
text: Tormentum - Dark Sorrow is a game that puts you into the shoes of a man that was given a chance at redemption, A chance to redeem your soul or to perish in the all consuming fire. Tormentum - Dark Sorrow proves to me that games that were funded by the fans via kickstarter are shaping up to be some of the best games in recent years and Tormentum - Dark Sorrow is definitely one of those games. The Music: I really liked the music allot in this game and it definitely fit the tone and atmosphere the devs were aiming for. The Art style: The visuals and artistic style of Tormentum are really cool and unique and are really pleasing to the eyes and to the senses. The Puzzles: Most of the puzzles are easy but satisfying to complete and you can find everything to complete your obstacles without having to go on a wild goose chase for everything. The Story: I thought the story was interesting and entertaining and i would like to go back to change some of the decisions i made. Game length: Tormentum is kinda short but it didn't feel like it needed to be a longer game to get its message across. Cast of Characters: The characters you meet in Tormentum are very unique and intriguing. Overall i would say that Tormentum is a cool and intriguing game with one of the coolest art styles i have seen in an adventure game, if you love adventure games and dark fantasy like myself i know you will like it to. I rate Tormentum 90 out of 100 points.

title: Tormentum - Dark Sorrow
text: Writing this as an adventure game veteran there is literally only one reason to play Tormentum: You like spooky art drawn in a Geigeresque fashion. Everything else that makes an adventure game good - well thought out puzzles, a good story, and an interesting protagonist - are missing here. The puzzles are very straight forward. You will only get stymied on the non-contextual puzzles - stuff like solving a rubik's puzzle or a literal jigsaw puzzle. Or on areas that require a keycode and you need to find where that password is randomly scrawled in the background. The story is a journey through the artist's conception of purgatory. There is a moral choice system, but you will frequently accidently pick the wrong option not realizing that this WAS a choice that affects the game's ending. Not that it really matters as you can probably finish the whole thing in 6 hours on your first play through. There's not really anything in the way of character development. The complete lack of voice acting is an extreme detractor for a 2016 adventure game. But if you like lots of pictures of skeletons, sinew, and tendons then this is the game for you. I'd rather play Deponia, Monkey Island, or any of the classic LucasArts games.

title: Tormentum - Dark Sorrow
text: I played through Tormentum in three short sessions spread out over a couple of evenings and I really enjoying the game. All the puzzles are logical and probably won't tax people's grey matter too much, but it all comes together so well - and it's a pleasure to explore the world. I think the difficulty is perfect for an enjoyable, frustration free, experience that requires just enough thought to keep you engaged. Everything is very well designed and readable. The art is great with big nods to Giger and Beksiński. But the artwork mostly avoids simply being derivative of the inspiration and manages to stand on its own. The sound design is also quite good, with atmospheric music that never outstays its welcome. This game is the school example of short game length not necessarily being bad. I enjoyed every second of it and by the end it felt like a complete experience (and there's reason to play it again). There's no unnecessary filler and the game is paced almost perfectly. I respect a game that respects my time.
